I am an engineer and while I don't design car seats I can tell you that everything we design is made with a list of assumptions and certain safety factors. in the case of a powered car seat for instance consider a few design constraints: people expect the seat to move quietly and within a certain amount of time, this means that your motor has to provide a certain amount of torque and not be too noisy which means lower RPM range. you also are constrained to 12 V and 10 to 15 amps of current. which means the motor can provide at most about 200 watts of usable work. This would work well for moving a load of about 200 lbs a few cm. if you now place a 400 lbs person in the seat, not only does the motor have to do a lot more work but there is increased friction in the mechanisms that transfer motion from the motor to the seat, thereby needing more power from the motor. If you wanted to make a seat with a motor powerful enough to suit most fats, you would have to have a dedicated power supply drawing power from the battery and perhaps stepping up the voltage so you could deliver more power to the motor. this could easily increase the cost of the car by $100 or more which means that either the consumers or the car company would eat hundreds of millions more in costs over the life of program just to accommodate a few lazy fats.
